rules.title: Class names in PascalCase
rules.why: Java classes are named in PascalCase (LoginPage, UserApiClient). Other styles make classes look like variables or constants and make the code base harder to search.
rules.before:
public class login_page { }
public class userapi { }
rules.after:
public class LoginPage { }
public class UserApi { }

rules.title: Method names in camelCase
rules.why: Methods are named in camelCase, starting lower case (clickLogin). Underscores, upper-case starts and all-caps names hide which methods exist when people search for one to reuse.
rules.before:
public void Click_Login() { ... }
public void ENTERUSER(String u) { ... }
rules.after:
public void clickLogin() { ... }
public void enterUsername(String username) { ... }

rules.title: Constants in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
rules.why: static final values are constants and are named in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, so a reader sees at once that the value never changes and can be shared.
rules.before:
private static final String loginUrl = "/login";
static final int timeout = 30;
rules.after:
private static final String LOGIN_URL = "/login";
static final int TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30;

rules.title: Fields, parameters and variables in camelCase
rules.why: Fields, parameters and local variables are named in camelCase. Underscores and upper-case names look like constants or classes.
rules.before:
String User_Name = "ada";
Locator Submit_Btn = page.locator("#submit");
rules.after:
String userName = "ada";
Locator submitButton = page.locator("#submit");

rules.title: Package names in lower case
rules.why: Package names are all lower case (com.company.pages). Mixed case breaks on case-insensitive file systems (Windows, macOS) and differs from every library you use.
rules.before:
package com.company.Pages;
package com.company.API_Utils;
rules.after:
package com.company.pages;
package com.company.api.utils;

rules.title: Names that say what the method does
rules.why: Names such as test1, method2, doIt or temp say nothing about what the method does. Nobody finds them when looking for something to reuse, so they write a new one: this is how duplicate methods start.
rules.before:
public void method2() { /* logs in */ }
public String temp(String s) { /* trims, lower-cases */ }
rules.after:
public void logInAs(User user) { ... }
public String normaliseEmail(String email) { ... }

rules.title: Method names start with a verb
rules.why: A method does something, so its name starts with a verb (clickSave, getTotal, isVisible). Consistent verbs (click, enter, select, get, verify) make methods easy to find with auto-complete.
rules.before:
public void loginButton() { ... }
public void userDetails(String id) { ... }
rules.after:
public void clickLoginButton() { ... }
public UserDetails fetchUserDetails(String id) { ... }

rules.title: No fixed waits (Thread.sleep, waitForTimeout)
rules.why: A fixed wait is either too short (the test fails when the app is slow: flaky) or too long (every run is slower). Playwright already waits for elements before acting, and web-first assertions retry until the condition holds.
rules.after:
page.locator("#save").click();
assertThat(page.locator(".toast")).hasText("Saved"); // retries up to the timeout

rules.title: No deprecated Playwright APIs
rules.why: Deprecated methods (waitForNavigation, type, waitForSelector) are racy or will be removed. Their replacements wait for the right condition.
rules.before:
page.waitForNavigation(() -> page.click("#next"));
page.locator("#q").type("shoes");

rules.title: Use locators instead of page.click(selector)
rules.why: page.click(selector), page.fill(selector, ...) and similar are discouraged: a Locator is defined once (in the page object), re-resolved on every use and works with web-first assertions.
rules.before:
page.fill("#username", user);
page.click("#login");

rules.title: Short methods that do one thing
rules.why: A long method usually does several things (log in, search, check the result). Each part cannot be reused on its own, so people copy the part they need: duplicates. Split it into named steps.

rules.title: Few parameters: group them in an object
rules.why: With many parameters, callers mix up their order (two Strings swap without any error) and every new field changes every caller. A record or a builder names each value.
rules.before: public void createUser(String first, String last, String email, String phone, String city, boolean admin) { ... }

rules.title: Classes with one responsibility
rules.why: A class with very many methods (CommonUtils, BaseTest with everything) is a place where people add instead of search. Split it by topic: DateUtils, StringUtils, page objects per page.
rules.before:
public class CommonUtils { // 120 methods: dates, strings, files, waits, API calls
}

rules.title: No static mutable Playwright/REST state
rules.why: A static non-final Page, Browser, RequestSpecification, Response or collection is shared by all tests. When tests run in parallel they overwrite each other's browser or response: random failures. Give each scenario its own instance (dependency injection such as PicoContainer, or ThreadLocal).

rules.title: Utility classes are final with a private constructor
rules.why: A class with only static methods is never meant to be created or extended. Make it final with a private constructor, so nobody writes new CommonUtils() or a subclass.

rules.title: No hard-coded URLs
rules.why: A URL in code ties the tests to one environment. Read base URLs from configuration (per environment) and keep only the path in code.
rules.before:
page.navigate("https://qa.myapp.com/login");
given().baseUri("https://qa-api.myapp.com")
rules.after:
page.navigate(config.uiBaseUrl() + "/login");
given().spec(apiSpec)   // base URI from config

rules.title: Repeated strings as constants or enums
rules.why: The same string written many times (a status, a header name, a role) is easy to mistype and hard to change. Use a constant, or an enum when it is one of a fixed set of values.

rules.title: No locators in step definitions
rules.why: Step definitions describe behaviour; page objects know the page. Locators in steps are copied to every step that touches the element, and a changed id must be fixed in many places.

rules.title: One locator, one place
rules.why: The same selector defined in several classes is a duplicate in disguise: when the page changes, some copies get fixed and others do not. Define it once in the page object (or a locator file) and reuse it.

rules.title: Then steps assert something
rules.why: A Then step that does not assert passes whatever the application does, so the scenario can never fail on it.

rules.title: Tests assert something
rules.why: A @Test without any assertion only checks that nothing threw an exception.

rules.title: No absolute or positional XPath
rules.why: /html/body/div[2]/div[1]/button breaks with every layout change. Prefer user-facing locators (getByRole, getByLabel, getByTestId) or a stable id.
rules.before: page.locator("/html/body/div[2]/div[1]/form/button[2]").click();
rules.after:
page.getByRole(AriaRole.BUTTON, new Page.GetByRoleOptions().setName("Save")).click();
page.getByTestId("save-button").click();

rules.title: No unused step definitions
rules.why: A step definition that no feature file uses is dead code, and often an old copy of a step that is written differently now. Delete it or reuse it.
rules.before:
@When("user clicks on login button")   // no feature uses this any more
public void clickLogin() { ... }
rules.after: // deleted; features use: When I log in as "ada"

rules.title: Shared request setup with RequestSpecBuilder
rules.why: Base URI, content type, auth and common headers written in every request method are copies: a new header must be added everywhere. Build one RequestSpecification and reuse it with spec(...).

rules.title: Check the response of a request
rules.why: A method that sends a request, does not check it and does not return it hides errors: a 500 or 401 goes unnoticed. Check the status (or return the response so the caller checks it).

rules.title: No empty catch blocks
rules.why: An empty catch hides the failure: the test goes on in a wrong state and fails later with a misleading error, or passes when it should fail.

rules.title: Do not swallow broad exceptions
rules.why: catch (Exception e) that only logs turns every problem (a typo, a timeout, a 500) into a passing step. Catch the specific exception you expect, or let it fail the test.

rules.title: Log exceptions instead of printStackTrace
rules.why: printStackTrace writes to stderr, outside the test report and without the scenario name; in parallel runs the traces of different tests mix.

rules.title: Use a logger instead of System.out
rules.why: System.out cannot be filtered by level, has no time or thread, and does not reach the test report. A logger (SLF4J) or the report API (scenario.log) does.
rules.before: System.out.println("Clicked login");
rules.after:
private static final Logger LOG = LoggerFactory.getLogger(LoginPage.class);

LOG.info("Clicked login");

rules.title: Enum and switch instead of if-else on strings
rules.why: A chain of if (x.equals("chrome")) else if (x.equals("firefox")) ... accepts any typo and grows in every copy. An enum lists the allowed values once, and a switch expression on it is checked by the compiler.

rules.title: Optional instead of returning null
rules.why: A method that returns null for "not found" forces every caller to remember a null check; a forgotten one is a NullPointerException far from the cause. Optional says it in the signature.

rules.title: StringBuilder or String.join in loops
rules.why: s += x in a loop creates a new string every time. StringBuilder, String.join or Collectors.joining are faster and clearer.
rules.after: String names = users.stream().map(User::name).collect(Collectors.joining(","));
